title: IAM Evaluation Drill
intro: Twelve scenario questions on policy evaluation, boundaries, roles and cross-account access. Answer cold — the explanation appears after each choice.
footer: Drawn from Lab 07 — How IAM actually decides. Reference notes: exam-notes.md
notes_intro: Twelve SAA-C03-style questions on how IAM evaluates a request, then the traps and reference tables. Answers are at the bottom — try them cold first.

questions.q: A role has an identity policy allowing `s3:*`. The bucket's resource policy contains an explicit Deny for that role's ARN. The role also has AdministratorAccess attached. Can it read the bucket?
options: Yes — AdministratorAccess overrides resource policies
No — an explicit Deny anywhere overrides every Allow
Yes — identity policies take precedence over resource policies
Only if the request comes from inside the VPC
questions.why: Explicit deny wins, always. It is evaluated first and nothing overrides it — not AdministratorAccess, not the account root, not a resource policy allow. This is the first rule of IAM evaluation and the most reliably tested one.

questions.q: A role has an identity policy allowing `s3:*` and `ec2:*`, and a permission boundary allowing only `s3:Get*` and `s3:List*`. What can the role actually do?
options: Everything in the identity policy — boundaries only apply to users
Only s3:Get* and s3:List* — the intersection of policy and boundary
Everything in the boundary, plus ec2:*
Nothing, because the two conflict
questions.why: Effective permissions are the intersection of the identity policy and the boundary. The boundary is a ceiling that grants nothing on its own — every EC2 action and every S3 write falls outside it and is denied, even though the identity policy plainly allows them.

questions.q: A permission boundary allowing `s3:*` is attached to a role that has no identity policy at all. What can the role do?
options: Everything in S3, since the boundary allows it
Nothing — a boundary grants no permissions
Only read operations in S3
Everything, because an empty identity policy means unrestricted
questions.why: A boundary only ever subtracts. With no identity policy there is nothing to intersect with, so the effective permission set is empty and the role can do nothing. Treating a boundary as a way to grant access is the classic misunderstanding.

questions.q: A team must be able to create IAM roles for their applications without being able to grant those roles more access than the security team permits. What is the standard approach?
options: Grant them iam:* and audit role creation with CloudTrail
Require a permission boundary on any role they create, enforced by a condition on iam:CreateRole
Give them read-only IAM access and create roles on their behalf
Apply a service control policy to their IAM user
questions.why: A condition requiring iam:PermissionsBoundary on CreateRole means every role they create is capped, whatever policy they attach. This is the canonical use of boundaries: delegating role creation without enabling privilege escalation. Auditing after the fact does not prevent it.

questions.q: An EC2 instance in Account A must read an S3 bucket in Account B. What is the recommended mechanism?
options: Create an IAM user in Account B and put its access keys on the instance
A role in Account B that the instance's role assumes, or a bucket policy granting the instance role
Make the bucket public and restrict by IP
Enable cross-region replication into Account A
questions.why: Either cross-account role assumption — a role in B trusting A, assumed via STS — or a bucket policy in B naming the instance's role directly. Both avoid long-lived credentials. Access keys on an instance are the anti-pattern the instance role exists to eliminate.

questions.q: The policy simulator reports `implicitDeny` for an action. What does that mean?
options: A policy explicitly denied the action
No policy allowed the action, so the default deny applies
The simulator could not evaluate the request
A service control policy blocked it
questions.why: Implicit deny is the default: nothing granted the action. Explicit deny means a policy actively forbade it. They need different fixes — an implicit deny is solved by adding an allow, an explicit deny by finding and removing the Deny statement, which no amount of additional allows will overcome.

questions.q: A company has 40 teams and wants each to manage only its own EC2 instances, without writing 40 policies. Which approach fits best?
options: One IAM group per team with a team-specific policy
Attribute-based access control using tag conditions
A permission boundary per team
One shared role with a very long policy listing every instance
questions.why: ABAC matches aws:ResourceTag/team against aws:PrincipalTag/team in a single policy that works for every team — including teams that do not exist yet. The trade-off is that tagging discipline becomes a security control. Role-per-team is correct but multiplies the policies to maintain.

questions.q: Which credential type does an application running on EC2 receive when it uses an instance profile?
options: A permanent access key and secret stored in the instance metadata
Temporary credentials that are automatically rotated
The credentials of the user who launched the instance
A password stored in Secrets Manager
questions.why: The instance profile delivers temporary credentials via STS, retrieved from the instance metadata service and rotated automatically before expiry. Nothing long-lived exists to leak or rotate — which is exactly why instance roles beat access keys in every scenario the exam presents.

questions.q: An SCP attached to an account denies `s3:DeleteBucket`. A user in that account has AdministratorAccess. Can they delete a bucket?
options: Yes — AdministratorAccess is evaluated after SCPs
No — an SCP sets a ceiling the account cannot exceed, including for root
Only if they use the root user
Only from the AWS console, not the CLI
questions.why: A service control policy is a ceiling on an entire account in an Organization. It grants nothing and cannot be overridden from inside the account — including by the account root user. Like a permission boundary, it only ever subtracts.

questions.q: A role's trust policy determines what?
options: What actions the role may perform
Which principals are allowed to assume the role
Which resources the role may access
How long the role's credentials remain valid
questions.why: The trust policy (the assume-role policy document) says who may become the role. The permission policy says what the role may do once assumed. Both must permit the operation: a principal with sts:AssumeRole still fails if the trust policy does not name it.

questions.q: Within a single account, an IAM role has no S3 permissions in its identity policy, but a bucket policy explicitly allows that role to GetObject. Can it read the object?
options: No — the identity policy must also allow it
Yes — within one account, an allow in either policy is sufficient
Only if the bucket is in the same region
Only if the role has s3:ListBucket as well
questions.why: Within the same account, an allow in the identity policy or the resource policy is enough. This is why S3 access can appear from nowhere when reading only the identity side. Cross-account is different: both the resource policy in the target account and the identity policy in the caller's account must allow it.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between an IAM role and an IAM user?
options: Roles are for AWS services, users are for people — nothing else differs
A user has long-lived credentials; a role is assumed and issues temporary credentials
Roles cannot have policies attached
Users can be assumed by services, roles cannot
questions.why: A user is an identity with long-lived credentials — a password and/or access keys. A role has no credentials of its own: principals assume it and receive temporary STS credentials that expire. Current best practice is to avoid users almost entirely, using federation or instance/service roles instead.
